objectives: Reach a settlement by Round 4 that the Council can approve on schedule (by June), avoiding the costs and precedential mess of an unagreed modification followed by UK retaliation

Preserve the maximum feasible UK-specific quota allocation and administration method that keeps the measure defensible against overcapacity concerns while giving the UK enough certainty that its steel industry is not facing open-ended global first-come first-served competition

Prevent the UK from joining Japan and Korea in a coordinated FTA dispute or in disapplying FTA provisions in retaliation — this means keeping the EU-UK FTA disapplication provision as a live negotiating chip rather than a fait accompli
Manage the interaction with the UK's own Article XXVIII process so that treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure is linked to, and improves alongside, what the EU offers the UK

Protect the EU's long-term credibility in the WTO: conduct a clean, procedurally sound Article XXVIII process so the modification is seen as legitimate, and preserve working relationships in Geneva across other files

Avoid setting precedents in the UK settlement (large country-specific quotas, low out-of-quota rates, broad carve-outs) that will be claimed by Turkey, Korea, India and Japan in their parallel processes
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settlement both capitals accept within four rounds: a UK country-specific quota allocation sized defensibly against UK trade flows, an administration method the UK can sell domestically, modest and targeted compensation elsewhere in the schedule, linkage that keeps EU exporters' treatment under the UK measure at least at status quo, and no UK participation in a joint FTA dispute with Japan and Korea. Failure is no settlement — the EU proceeds unilaterally, the UK withdraws substantially equivalent concessions against €3.6m tonnes of EU steel exports, Japan and Korea succeed in recruiting the UK into a coordinated FTA dispute, and the EU's reputation in Geneva takes a hit that bleeds into other files. Partial failure is a settlement whose terms are so generous that they anchor the Turkey/Korea/India/Japan negotiations at levels the Council will not accept.
declaration.approach: Open by establishing procedure and tone: confirm the EU is negotiating in good faith, that the UK is recognised as a principal supplying interest, and that everything on the table is genuinely open. Do not lead with concessions — first map the UK's priorities (volume vs allocation method vs administration vs the FTA disapplication provision) before revealing EU flexibility. Signal early that the FTA disapplication provision is negotiable, because it is the cheapest high-value chip the EU holds and the most direct lever against the UK joining a joint dispute. Move toward a package built around: a UK-specific quota share calibrated to historic trade (something in the region of the UK's average exports, with the EU defending a figure below 2.4Mt and the UK pushing above the 400kt global quota), licensing or country-specific administration instead of first-come first-served, a review clause and duration to give the UK predictability, and explicit linkage to EU exporters' country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure. Resist on the out-of-quota rate and product carve-outs as long as possible — these are the precedents most damaging to the parallel claims. Throughout, keep the relationship with the UK counterpart professional and forward-looking, report honestly to Brussels, and never let the table believe the EU is indifferent to no-deal: the fallback exists but it is bad for both sides and I should say so plainly.

parties.who: UK Geneva counterpart (UK Mission to the WTO)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free access for UK steel: a large UK-specific quota (ideally at or near the 2.4Mt historic average), licensing or country-specific allocation rather than global first-come first-served, removal or softening of the FTA disapplication provision, a review clause, and protection of the TCA relationship. Will also want to show domestic political wins for steel-producing constituencies and may use the Japan/Korea joint dispute whisperings as leverage.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade, ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A package sellable as protecting the UK steel industry and jobs at a small number of high-profile sites; enough quota volume and certainty to avoid plant closures being blamed on government; reciprocal treatment for EU exporters under the UK measure kept as a bargaining chip; ministerial clearance only for a deal that looks like a clear win.

parties.who: European Commission / Brussels (my capital)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: The modification to proceed on schedule with a clean Article XXVIII process; compensation costs contained; no precedent that unravels the parallel Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims; Council-approvable terms; avoidance of UK retaliation against EU steel exports.

parties.who: EU Council / Trade Policy Committee / member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Split interests: steel-producing member states want a tight quota and high out-of-quota rate; steel-consuming manufacturing member states want cheaper imports and may tolerate a larger TRQ; all want the June timetable held.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India, Japan
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Country-specific allocations at least as favourable as anything the UK gets, referencing their larger volumes (Turkey, Korea) or FTA status (Japan, Korea); Japan and Korea reportedly want UK co-sponsorship of an FTA dispute; all will scrutinise the UK settlement as the anchor for their own claims.

parties.who: UK steel industry and affected communities
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Guaranteed, predictable access to the EU market at volumes close to historic levels; they are the political pressure behind the UK capital's red lines.

parties.who: EU steel industry
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A tight overall TRQ, high out-of-quota rate, no FTA carve-outs, and retention of their country-specific allocations in the UK market under the UK measure.

objectives: Secure Article XXVIII agreement in time for the June Council vote while preserving a genuinely restrictive steel import regime: high out-of-quota bound rate, tight TRQ, strong administration and anti-circumvention.

Keep the UK inside the process by offering just enough certainty of access to make acceptance rational, without converting the regime into a set of permanent country-specific rights that weaken EU control.

Avoid precedents that Turkey, Korea, India and Japan can exploit: no automatic country shares, no broad FTA carve-out beyond legally unavoidable EEA treatment, no review clause that reopens the regime quickly.
Use possible compensation only where it is cheap for the EU and does not stimulate import-sensitive opposition in the Council.

Exploit linkage cautiously: better treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure may justify UK access, but must not become a public quota-for-quota bargain that undermines the Article XXVIII rationale.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a same-round acceptance by both capitals before the deadline, Council approval on schedule, a durable legal basis for the regime, a material fall in vulnerable steel imports, no uncontrolled proliferation of FTA or country shares, limited EU compensation exposure, and no immediate UK/US retaliation spiral. Failure is slippage past June, a hollowed-out TRQ through volume creep or carve-outs, precedents that strengthen other claimants, heavy compensation in sensitive sectors, UK withdrawal of concessions hitting EU exporters, or a deal that satisfies Geneva but collapses in the Council.
declaration.approach: Open firm on the notified architecture: 50% out-of-quota bound rate, 400,000 tonne TRQ, global first-come first-served administration, no early review, and disapplication of FTA reductions except where legally required for the EEA. Present this as a permanent, defensible response to non-market overcapacity rather than a negotiable safeguard auction. Make the UK price the cost of no agreement: loss of timetable, deeper exposure for its concentrated exports, and separate treatment from EEA partners. Trade only controlled concessions for early closure: marginal TRQ flexibility, licensing/administration predictability rather than guaranteed UK share, narrow product-line treatment for specialist grades, technical anti-circumvention cooperation, a distant review only if performance triggers are objective, and low-sensitivity tariff compensation. Keep any FTA-pool idea internal unless it buys acceptance without creating a large UK claim; a big UK share would trigger others and the Council. Coordinate messaging with member states: steel producers get assured restraint, downstream users get administration and targeted continuity, and capitals get a June-ready package.

parties.who: UK Geneva seat and UK capital / Department for Business and Trade
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free access to the EU, preferably a UK-specific or FTA preferential allocation, licensing certainty, carve-outs for UK product lines, preservation of TCA benefits, restraint on the proposed FTA disapplication, and linkage to continued EU access under the UK steel measure. They will threaten to walk and rebalance, but their export concentration and weaker no-deal position should push them toward settlement if given face-saving certainty.

parties.who: Council and Trade Policy Committee
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Steel-producing member states will want a tougher regime, low import volumes and quick implementation; steel-consuming member states will want supply security, manageable costs and no disruption to manufacturing. Collectively they require a defensible June package with no visible surrender to the UK.

parties.who: Commissioner and DG TRADE leadership
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A timely, legally robust conclusion that protects the measure, contains geopolitical escalation including US threats, avoids compensation inflation, and can be defended to the Council, Parliament, industry and trading partners.

parties.who: EU steel industry
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A materially tighter import regime, high out-of-quota protection, strict enforcement, no large UK or FTA carve-outs, and confidence that the Article XXVIII outcome permanently anchors the domestic measure.

parties.who: EU downstream steel users and manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Predictable access for grades not available in the EU, administrable quotas, no panic under first-come first-served, protection from price spikes, and targeted continuity rather than liberalization.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India and Japan
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Separate but watchful claims: preservation or expansion of their own access, resistance to any privileged UK/FTA pool, and exploitation of any country-share precedent. Larger suppliers will argue principal supplying interest and substantial compensation.

parties.who: United States
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Leverage over EU trade policy and a visible concession or pause; likely to use tariff threats to raise the EU cost of proceeding and to discourage discrimination or contagion.

parties.who: EEA members and other FTA partners
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: EEA members will insist on preserved treatment grounded in the EEA relationship; other FTA partners will resist erosion of preferences and object if the UK obtains a large share of any preferential pool.

parties.who: WTO membership and dispute environment
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Formal compliance with Article XXVIII process, credible compensation, and avoidance of measures that look like discriminatory quotas dressed as schedule modification; any perception of bad faith will weaken the EU position in parallel claims and disputes.

objectives: Secure an Article XXVIII outcome that preserves commercially meaningful, predictable tariff-free access for UK steel to the EU, preferably through a UK-specific allocation close to recent trade and/or carve-outs for the most exposed product lines.

Move the EU off 400,000 tonnes global first-come-first-served and 50% out-of-quota as the final architecture: seek larger volume, country-specific shares, licensing based on historic trade, staged administration, a materially lower or staged out-of-quota bound rate, duration with review, and removal or narrowing of the FTA-disapplication text as it affects the UK.
If steel access cannot be made whole, extract compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule that is real, usable by UK exporters, and timed to matter before adjustment costs bite.

Use the UK steel measure and EU exporters' existing country-specific quotas as leverage for reciprocity and orderly market access, without creating an indefensible WTO linkage or triggering a wider retaliation cycle.
Keep London accurately informed and obtain a settlement mandate before closing; do not imply UK acceptance beyond instructions.
Manage Japan and Korea so their proposed joint FTA dispute remains potential pressure rather than an early disruption that hardens the EU or damages the UK's Geneva credibility.
Protect the broader goods relationship with the Commission and other members so committees, schedule work and future negotiations remain functional after this file concludes.
declaration.success_and_failure: This goes well if, by the end of Round 4, both capitals accept the same package and that package gives the UK durable, bankable access covering most recent UK steel exports through country-specific volume, carve-outs or equivalent compensation; limits the practical effect of the 50% bound rate; removes or greatly narrows the FTA-disapplication risk for UK-origin steel; includes administration industry can plan around, a review/sunset mechanism, and a managed interface with the UK steel measure. It also goes well if no settlement is reached but London has a clear record of EU positions, a tested fall-back and retaliation analysis, preserved alliances, and no avoidable damage to other files. It goes badly if the EU proceeds on 400,000 tonnes global first-come-first-served at 50% with FTA disapplication intact, the UK is forced into delayed and weak rebalancing, UK steel sites face cliff-edge loss of EU demand, I overstate authority or misreport the landing zone, or Japan/Korea manoeuvres and UK/EU linkage turn this into a wider dispute that outruns the June timeline.
declaration.approach: Open firm, technical and time-aware: acknowledge the EU's overcapacity problem and June constraint, but make clear the notified design is not a negotiable basis for a principal supplier whose trade is concentrated and whose industry faces the same non-market shock. Put a complete package on the table early rather than bidding line-by-line: UK country-specific quota anchored to the three-year average with carve-outs for EU-scarce grades; licensing against historic import contracts in quarterly tranches; strict melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention discipline; in-quota zero duty; out-of-quota bound rate reduced or staged with a review against overcapacity indicators; duration and review; removal or UK-specific neutralisation of the FTA-disapplication clause; and a compensation menu only for residual loss. Signal that the UK is separately calibrating its own steel measure and that EU exporters' access there will be easier to stabilise if UK access to the EU is stabilised, while keeping that as reciprocity rather than an explicit threat. Probe what the Commission can actually sell to the Trade Policy Committee and which member states are driving volume versus administration. In consultations, give London options, red lines and the cost of no-deal, and request a settlement figure rather than improvising one. Keep Japan and Korea close enough to amplify risk for the EU, but do not let them set UK timing or convert this into an FTA dispute before the Article XXVIII landing zone is known.

parties.who: European Commission Geneva counterpart / DG Trade negotiator
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A mandate-compliant, quick conclusion before June; defensible protection against non-market overcapacity; no precedent that invites Turkey, Korea, India and Japan to expand claims; minimal retaliation and dispute risk; enough flexibility to show the Council the package is balanced between steel-producing and steel-consuming member states.

parties.who: EU Council, Trade Policy Committee and key member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producer member states will want a tight quota, high out-of-quota protection and weak review language; consuming and manufacturing member states will want adequate import supply and predictable licensing; all will want legal safety, schedule discipline and a vote that can pass on time.

parties.who: London: Department for Business and Trade, ministers and UK steel policy leads
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Avoid destruction of UK steel capacity, secure maximum EU access or equivalent value, keep control of any settlement, understand the EU's true bottom line, retain credible rebalancing options if talks fail, and avoid being bounced by Geneva, industry, Japan/Korea or the EU timeline.

parties.who: UK steel producers and affected site communities
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Volume near recent exports, country-specific certainty rather than global first-come-first-served, product-level protection for hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod exposure, early clarity before investment and employment decisions, and no cosmetic compensation that cannot be used.

parties.who: UK downstream steel users and importers of EU steel
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: No self-defeating UK retaliation that raises input costs, continuity of EU supply under the UK measure, and a settlement that does not swap a steel crisis for a manufacturing cost shock.

parties.who: Japan and Korea
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Pull the UK toward a joint FTA dispute and possible disapplication of FTA benefits to raise pressure on the EU, while keeping their own Article XXVIII claims separate and extracting maximum advantage from any UK-EU friction.

parties.who: Turkey and India and other reserved-rights members
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Protect or enlarge their own access and resist any EU-UK arrangement that consumes too much of the quota pool, creates discrimination they can challenge, or sets a template that limits their compensation.

parties.who: WTO Secretariat and Geneva committee counterparts
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Procedural correctness under Article XXVIII, no avoidable dispute escalation, and a UK that remains reliable, transparent and constructive across the wider goods agenda.

objectives: Secure the largest possible guaranteed zero-duty access to the EU for UK steel, ideally through a UK-specific quota close to recent export volumes and reflecting the UK's product mix, with a first preference for at least 2.4 million tonnes and a realistic landing zone materially above any residual share of a 400,000-tonne global quota.
Remove or neutralise the proposed disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel and preserve the practical value of the EU-UK TCA.

Achieve a predictable and administrable allocation method, preferably a UK country-specific quota with licensing or another system that prevents front-loading and displacement by third-country exporters.
Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate below 50% wherever possible and secure carve-outs for products where the UK is especially exposed or where EU supply is limited.
Build in duration, review and adjustment provisions that allow the arrangement to be improved if market conditions change or if the EU's safeguard architecture is revised.

Use the UK's own steel safeguard, including improved EU country-specific quota allocations, only as leverage for significant and verifiable EU concessions, while retaining enough domestic protection to keep the two at-risk plants viable.

Keep open the option of compensation on other EU tariff lines or equivalent commercially meaningful commitments if the EU cannot deliver sufficient steel access, but do not substitute peripheral concessions for a viable steel outcome unless ministers judge the overall package indispensable.

Preserve the UK's legal position if no settlement is reached, including the ability to withdraw substantially equivalent concessions and to continue coordination with other affected members where useful.
declaration.success_and_failure: This goes well if the final package gives UK producers dependable, preferential zero-duty access on a scale sufficient to persuade the owners of the two at-risk plants to keep investing, while avoiding an outcome in which the UK gives away safeguard quota for little in return. A good outcome also leaves ministers able to defend the deal as protecting steel jobs, preserving the TCA in practice, and maintaining leverage over future EU measures. It goes badly if the EU retains a small global first-come quota, disapplies FTA preferences against UK steel, or secures improved access to the UK market without commensurate guaranteed access for UK exports. Failure also includes any deal that looks technically tidy but is politically indefensible because it does not keep the plants open, or any negotiating line that boxes ministers into accepting symbolic concessions elsewhere as a substitute for a viable steel settlement.
declaration.approach: I will treat the EU's proposal as a starting point for compensation under Article XXVIII, not as the baseline against which marginal improvements should be measured. My approach is to link every UK move to a concrete EU move: no improved EU quota under the UK safeguard without a UK-specific quota, better product coverage, and a lower out-of-quota rate in return. I will keep the subsidy option and possible rebalancing rights private, avoid signalling desperation over plant closures, and present country-specific allocation as a pragmatic administration method rather than a favour to the UK. I will use the UK's concentrated product exposure, the mutual interest in orderly steel trade, the EU's need for Council agreement by June, and the risk of UK retaliation to press for a durable package. I will keep instructions to Geneva tight on priorities but leave enough room to trade across volume, allocation, rate, duration, review and selected compensation lines. I will not accept a package merely because it is available in time; ministerial clearance will depend on whether the package can be defended as keeping the industry alive.

parties.who: UK Geneva seat
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A clear negotiating mandate, room to test EU flexibility, and early guidance on which trade-offs are acceptable so they can move quickly between rounds without overstepping ministerial clearance.

parties.who: EU Geneva seat
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A legally defensible Article XXVIII settlement that can be sold to Brussels as stable and compensated, while preserving as much of the 50% bound rate and restrictive quota architecture as possible.

parties.who: European Commission and Council
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: An agreement that can be concluded by June, avoids retaliation, keeps member states with steel producers and steel users aligned, and does not unravel the wider steel measure or parallel negotiations with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan.

parties.who: EU member states with significant steel production
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Strong protection against import pressure, limited preferential treatment for the UK, and no precedent that weakens the EU's response to global overcapacity.

parties.who: EU member states with major steel-consuming manufacturers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Reliable access to UK and other imported steel, lower input costs, and an allocation system that avoids supply disruption and administrative bottlenecks.

parties.who: UK steel producers and owners of the two at-risk plants
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Guaranteed, bankable EU access at commercially viable volumes, protection against being crowded out by third countries, and confidence that the government will not trade away their core market for minor concessions elsewhere.

parties.who: UK downstream steel users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Continued access to EU steel at predictable prices and no abrupt tightening of the UK safeguard that raises input costs or disrupts supply chains.

parties.who: UK ministers and the Secretary of State
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically saleable outcome that protects steel jobs, can be presented as standing up for UK industry, and avoids either a visible capitulation or an unmanaged trade conflict with the EU.

parties.who: Other UK government departments
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A settlement consistent with wider EU-UK relations, subsidy-control constraints, trade remedy policy, and the UK's own Article XXVIII and safeguard processes.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India and Japan
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Protection of their own Article XXVIII claims and resistance to any EU-UK arrangement that absorbs too much quota or sets an unfavourable precedent for their negotiations.

parties.who: EU exporters to the UK
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Preservation or improvement of their country-specific quota allocations under the UK safeguard and avoidance of retaliatory UK withdrawals if talks fail.

public_message: Thank you. The Union has notified its intention to modify its schedule on these 41 lines under Article XXVIII, and that process will proceed. Our notification stands as our opening position: a bound rate of 50% ad valorem, with a tariff rate quota of 400,000 tonnes per year at zero duty, allocated globally on a first-come first-served basis. We recognise the United Kingdom holds a principal supplying interest and we are here to negotiate seriously and in good faith. I would note several things. First, we are conscious of the Council timeline and would like to conclude by June; that should concentrate minds on both sides. Second, while the volume and headline rate in the notification define our opening, the Union is prepared to discuss how the quota is allocated and administered, its duration and review arrangements, the treatment of specific product lines, and the broader compensation package. We see the design of the final regime as part of this negotiation, not a fixed backdrop. Third, I would ask that we keep this process within Article XXVIII. Matters concerning the interpretation or disapplication of our respective FTAs are best resolved through the bilateral channels those agreements provide, not through parallel dispute action, which would complicate this negotiation and the wider relationship. I would welcome the UK's opening position, including its views on allocation, volumes, and where it sees scope for an overall package.

other_terms: Open to discussing allocation method (global vs country-specific) and administration (FCFS vs licensing) as part of the package
Open to a review clause and defined duration
Open to discussing product-line carve-outs and compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule
FTA treatment to be addressed through bilateral TCA channels, not FTA dispute action
June conclusion target to allow Council vote on schedule

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A firm rejection of the 400,000 tonne global FCFS pool, a demand for a country-specific UK tranche reflecting historical trade (they will anchor near their 2.4 Mt annual export average, which exceeds the entire pool), objections to the 50% out-of-quota rate, and strong pressure on the FTA disapplication language.
expectations.why: UK exports of 2.4 Mt against a 400,000 tonne global pool makes FCFS catastrophic for them; a UK-specific tranche is their obvious core ask. The FTA disapplication directly targets UK-originating steel and will be a red line.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Leverage signals referencing the UK's own Article XXVIII process, the EU's 3.6 Mt of exports into the UK market, and possible coordination with Japan and Korea on FTA dispute action.
expectations.why: The UK holds reciprocal leverage through its own steel measure and EU country-specific quotas under it, and we have indications Japan and Korea are encouraging joint FTA dispute action. They will test whether the threat moves us.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Instructions to hold near the notification in Round 1, gather the UK's bottom line, and preserve flexibility on allocation and the FTA language as tradable items for later rounds.
expectations.why: No settlement figure has been given; the mandate is to conduct the process and report. Early concessions would be criticised by steel-producing member states before the Council vote.

private_rationale: Opening at the notified position is the only defensible start absent a settlement figure from Brussels: any early movement on the pool or the rate would be read by member states as giving away the compensation space before knowing the UK's asks. The genuine flexibilities I signal — allocation method, administration, duration/review, carve-outs, compensation — cost nothing now and are exactly the currency needed to buy a UK-specific tranche or FTA language concessions later. I explicitly warn against FTA dispute action because a UK-Japan-Korea joint dispute is the worst-case spillover; framing it as out-of-scope early gives me a record to point back to. Offering a review clause and an 8-year duration in the opening is a cheap goodwill gesture that creates negotiating room without touching volume or rate. I keep uk_tranche null because conceding a country-specific share in Round 1 would collapse the global-allocation position Turkey and Korea (larger shippers) will resist, and it must be traded, not given.

public_message: Thank you, and I echo your commitment to conclude this seriously and in good faith — we are equally conscious of the June timeline. Let me be direct about where the notified position leaves us. A global first-come first-served quota of 400,000 tonnes provides the United Kingdom with no guaranteed access whatsoever. You will know as well as I do that other suppliers ship larger volumes into your market than we do; on a first-come basis the pool would be exhausted early in each quota year, and UK product would face the 50% rate in practice regardless of the zero-duty tranche on paper. Given that 2.4 million tonnes and roughly three quarters of UK steel exports by value go to the EU, the notified design is functionally a prohibitive tariff on the UK industry. That cannot be the basis of substantially equivalent compensation under Article XXVIII, and I want to be clear with you now that it sits nowhere near a landing zone. I welcome your indication that allocation, administration, duration and the broader package are genuinely open, because that is where this negotiation will be won or lost. On that basis, the UK's opening position is as follows. First, the quota must be allocated on a country-specific basis, set by reference to historical trade over a representative period — we propose the 2022–24 average. Second, the total pool must reflect actual import demand on these lines, not a fraction of it: we propose five million tonnes. Third, within that pool, a UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes, consistent with our reference-period trade. Fourth, administration by import licensing with periodic allocation, so that access is predictable rather than a race at the port. Fifth, duration of three years with a review clause — a measure justified by a temporary overcapacity shock should not be permanent by default. Sixth — and I want to flag this as a matter of real concern — the proposed legal text disapplying FTA tariff reductions on originating steel. The UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement provides for zero tariffs on originating goods. Stripping that preference for steel, in a measure whose stated rationale is non-market-economy overcapacity — a rationale which, as you know, applies to neither of us and which our own industries both face from the same third-country sources — is not something we can accept. Our position is that TCA preferential treatment is preserved: UK-origin steel above the tranche enters at the TCA rate, not the 50% bound rate. Finally, on scope: we would want to discuss carve-outs for product lines where EU domestic supply is insufficient to meet downstream demand. I would also note, as you did, that this negotiation does not exist in isolation. The UK is running its own Article XXVIII process on its own steel measure, under which EU exporters currently hold country-specific quota allocations in our market — a market that took 3.6 million tonnes of EU steel last year. We are prepared to discuss the treatment of EU exporters under that measure as part of the overall package here, and coherence between the two regimes seems to us plainly in both sides' interest. I would rather reach that coherence by agreement than by arithmetic. On your third point: we agree this should be concluded within Article XXVIII, and I am not here to litigate. But it was the Union's own proposal that placed FTA treatment on the table, and the UK reserves all its rights under the TCA in that regard. I look forward to hearing where the Union's flexibility actually lies on allocation and volume.

other_terms: TCA preferential treatment preserved: UK-origin steel above the UK tranche enters at the TCA rate of 0%, not the 50% bound rate; EU to drop proposed legal text disapplying FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel
Country-specific shares set by reference to 2022-24 average historical trade
Administration by import licensing with periodic (e.g. quarterly) allocation, not first-come first-served
Carve-outs from the measure for specific product lines where EU domestic supply is insufficient to meet downstream demand

Reciprocal coherence with the UK's own steel measure and Article XXVIII process: treatment of EU exporters' country-specific quota allocations in the UK market to be addressed as part of the overall package
Enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions to be product- and origin-based and not to single out UK trade

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Rejection of the 5m tonne pool and 2.4m UK tranche as incompatible with the measure's protective purpose, but genuine engagement on allocation — they signalled allocation and administration are in their flexible zone. Expect them to probe whether country-specific allocation at a much smaller tranche could anchor a deal, and to resist hard on the TCA preference point while quietly acknowledging the targeted disapplication text is legally awkward for them.
expectations.why: Their opening framing deliberately separated 'volume and headline rate' (fixed-ish) from 'allocation and design' (negotiable), which tells me where their mandate has room. The June Council deadline means they cannot afford to stonewall on everything.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A split response in the Trade Policy Committee: steel-producing member states pushing to hold the pool down, steel-consuming member states and those with export exposure to the UK urging movement on allocation and the FTA text. Expect a modestly expanded mandate on allocation method by Round 2 or 3, not on volume.
expectations.why: The Commission needs a conclusion it can sell to both camps before June; allocation concessions cost producers less visibly than volume concessions.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Instructions to hold the line on country-specific allocation and the TCA point, with questions about how far I can trade down the pool and tranche figures, and whether to make the linkage to our own steel measure more explicit.
expectations.why: London gave me no settlement figure, so they will want my read of EU flexibility before authorising any movement.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Renewed pressure in the corridors to escalate jointly on the FTA disapplication text, especially once they hear I raised it at the table without threatening dispute action.

report: Round 1 was a formal exchange of opening positions, no movement on either side yet. I tabled the notified position (50% bound, 400kt global FCFS TRQ) and signalled — per my instructions — that allocation method, administration, duration/review, product carve-outs and the broader compensation package are genuinely open, while the modification itself will proceed. I also asked that FTA questions be kept out of parallel dispute channels. The UK responded with a maximalist but structured opening: (1) country-specific allocation on a 2022–24 historical reference period; (2) total pool of 5 million tonnes; (3) a UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes (i.e. their full current export volume, tariff-free); (4) administration by import licensing with periodic allocation; (5) three-year duration with a review clause; (6) preservation of TCA preference — UK-origin steel above the tranche would enter at the TCA rate, not the 50% bound rate, which in practice guts the out-of-quota rate for the UK entirely; (7) carve-outs where EU supply is insufficient; and (8) explicit linkage to their own Article XXVIII/steel measure, where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas into a 3.6mt market — offered as part of the package, with a pointed remark about reaching coherence 'by agreement rather than by arithmetic.' They stated flatly that the notified design is 'nowhere near a landing zone' and reserved all TCA rights on the FTA-disapplication text. Atmospherics were professional; the UK counterpart is clearly under instruction to conclude by June and wants a deal, but their opening asks for a regime that is preferential in all but name for UK steel.

recommendation.reasoning: This is the UK's opening ask, not a landing zone, and I have no settlement figure from Brussels against which to move. Accepting is impossible: 2.4mt duty-free plus TCA treatment above the tranche would leave the UK effectively outside the measure, which the Council will not approve and which would detonate the parallel Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims — Ankara and Seoul ship more than the UK and would demand equivalent treatment, collapsing the regime. Walking away is premature and costly: it guarantees UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions within six months against EU exporters, invites the joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute I have been hearing about, and poisons the committees where I must work with this counterpart for years. The right course is to negotiate toward a middle position: a meaningful but below-volume UK country-specific tranche within a larger (but far below 5mt) pool, licensing administration (acceptable to us, low cost), a longer duration with review (trade duration for volume), and the FTA-disapplication text used as leverage — potentially softened or carved out for the UK in exchange for UK restraint on parallel dispute action and favourable treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure.

instruction: Good report. Round 2 is where we move, and you now have an envelope. Do not open at the ceiling. Line for Round 2: acknowledge that the notified FCFS design creates genuine unpredictability for established suppliers and signal that the Union is prepared to move to country-specific allocation based on a historical reference period — this is a real concession, present it as such. On volumes, reject 5mt/2.4mt outright as inconsistent with the purpose of the measure; open with a total pool of 2.2 million tonnes and a UK tranche of 800,000 tonnes, and make clear the UK tranche is a share of a pool that must also accommodate Turkey, Korea, India and Japan, whose volumes exceed the UK's. Administration: concede import licensing with periodic allocation early — it costs us nothing and the UK wants it badly; get credit for it. Duration: hold at five years minimum; a review clause is acceptable and you may offer it, but only in exchange for movement on volume — do not give it away. Out-of-quota rate: 50% stands; you have no authority below it. On the FTA-disapplication text: do not concede anything yet, but you may say the Union is 'prepared to examine how the measure interacts with existing preferential arrangements' if the UK confirms it will not initiate or join dispute proceedings under the TCA and if there is satisfactory treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure. Treat that text as the closing coin, not an opening one. On the UK linkage: you may discuss the treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure in parallel — signal we would expect existing EU country-specific allocations in the UK market to be preserved as part of any overall package. Do not accept the UK's framing that above-tranche UK steel enters at the TCA rate; that is a red line — it would exempt the UK from the measure entirely.

authority.notes: Open at 2.2mt total / 800kt UK tranche; ceilings are 3.0mt total / 1.2mt UK and may only be approached in Rounds 3–4 in exchange for the full package. FTA-disapplication text may be narrowed or made inapplicable to UK-origin steel ONLY as part of a final package that includes: (a) UK written confirmation of no TCA dispute action, (b) preservation of EU country-specific quota allocations under the UK steel measure at no less than current volumes, and (c) UK tranche at or below 1.2mt. report: Round 1 was an exchange of opening positions. The EU held its notification (50% bound, 400kt global first-come first-served TRQ) as its opening but explicitly signalled flexibility on allocation method, administration, duration, review arrangements, product carve-outs, and the broader compensation package, and confirmed it wants to conclude before the June Council vote. It also asked, pre-emptively, that FTA disapplication matters be kept out of this process and handled bilaterally — a clear defensive move against the Japan/Korea joint-dispute idea and against us pressing the TCA point. I tabled the UK's opening: 5Mt total pool allocated country-specifically on 2022–24 historical trade, a 2.4Mt UK tranche, licensing administration, three-year duration with review, carve-outs for short-supply product lines, preservation of TCA preferential treatment above the tranche, and linkage to the treatment of EU exporters under our own Article XXVIII steel measure (3.6Mt of EU steel into the UK market). I made clear the notified design is functionally prohibitive for the UK and sits nowhere near a landing zone, while confirming we want to conclude within Article XXVIII. Neither side moved off its opening; the EU has not yet revealed where its real flexibility lies on allocation and volume, which is the crux.

recommendation.reasoning: This was an opening round; neither side should or did move. Our bid is deliberately at the top of the range (full historical volume, full TCA preservation) to leave negotiating room — accepting anything now would be premature and nothing acceptable is yet on the table. Walking away after one round would forfeit the EU's stated flexibility and the leverage of its June deadline, and would leave us with the worst-case outcome: 400kt global FCFS, which exhausts early and gives the UK no guaranteed access. Out-of-quota rate of 0 reflects our position that TCA preferences are preserved for originating UK steel above the tranche; if we concede that red line, the fallback must still be well below 50%.

Reiterate that any regime without a guaranteed UK tranche is a non-starter and cannot constitute substantially equivalent compensation. Hold the 5Mt pool / 2.4Mt UK tranche / country-specific / licensing position intact. On the TCA point: maintain it firmly as a stated red line in the room — UK-origin steel above the tranche enters at the TCA rate. Do not hint that it is tradeable; if we eventually sell it, it must be sold very late and very dearly (think a UK tranche materially above 1.5Mt plus licensing plus review). On their request to keep FTA matters out: give no commitment either way; a courteous non-answer keeps the pressure on without escalation, and do not be seen coordinating with Japan or Korea at this stage. On the safeguard linkage: you may develop it, but positively — signal that an ambitious UK tranche and TCA-consistent treatment would allow us to be constructive on EU country-specific allocations under our own measure (they shipped 3.6Mt into us last year; they know what's at stake). Do not make explicit threats yet. Probe their interest in carve-outs for short-supply lines and compensation elsewhere in their schedule as package components, but concede nothing. Report back their counter before Round 3 with your read of their floor.

public_message: Thank you. The Union has reflected carefully on what you put on the table, and I am in a position to make the first substantive move of this negotiation. I will be candid about both the movement and the limits. First, on allocation: you made a persuasive case that a global first-come first-served design creates genuine unpredictability for established suppliers, whatever the merits of the headline volume. The Union is therefore prepared to move to country-specific allocation based on a historical reference period. I want to be clear that this is a significant concession from our notified position — it restructures the architecture of the regime, and it is offered on the understanding that it is recognised as such. Second, on administration: the Union can accept import licensing with periodic allocation. Predictable, orderly access serves our importers and downstream users as much as it serves your exporters, so we see no reason to contest it. Third, on volumes, and here I must be direct: five million tonnes for the pool and 2.4 million for the UK is not an opening this negotiation can build on. A pool of that size would empty the measure of effect, and a UK tranche at your full export volume would place the United Kingdom outside the regime altogether. The Council will not approve it, and I would ask you to reflect on what it would mean for the other members in this process, several of whom ship more into our market than you do and whose claims we are handling in parallel. Any country-specific architecture must accommodate them too. The Union's proposal is therefore a total pool of 2.2 million tonnes, with a UK tranche of 800,000 tonnes within it. I recognise that is well below your ask; it is a genuine opening, not a restatement of the notification, and there is a negotiation to be had between our two numbers. Fourth, on duration: the Union's position is five years, and we are prepared to include a review clause as part of an overall package — but I will be transparent that we see the review clause as something to be settled alongside the volume question, not separately from it. The out-of-quota bound rate of 50% stands; I have no flexibility there and it would save us both time to treat it as fixed. Fifth, on the TCA question. I heard your concern, and I will not pretend it away. The Union is prepared to examine how the measure interacts with existing preferential arrangements. But that examination can only happen in a particular context: confirmation from the United Kingdom that it will not initiate or join dispute proceedings under the TCA in relation to this measure, and a satisfactory outcome on the treatment of EU exporters under your own steel measure. On that last point, since you raised it: we are content to discuss the two regimes in parallel, and our expectation would be that existing EU country-specific allocations in the UK market — into a market that took 3.6 million tonnes of our steel last year — are preserved as part of any overall package. Coherence by agreement, as you put it, requires coherence in both directions. Finally, on carve-outs: we are willing to look at specific lines where EU supply is genuinely insufficient, on the basis of evidence, but this will be a narrow exercise, not a renegotiation of the scope. I would welcome your response on the volume architecture, because that is where this negotiation now lives.

private_rationale: Followed Brussels' instructions precisely: opened at 2.2mt/800kt rather than the ceiling, presented country-specific allocation as the headline concession (it genuinely restructures the regime and costs us nothing we weren't authorised to give), conceded licensing early for credit since it is costless, held 50% as fixed, held duration at five years with the review clause explicitly tied to volume movement rather than given away, and deployed the authorised conditional language on the FTA-disapplication text — 'prepared to examine how the measure interacts with existing preferential arrangements' — without conceding anything, keeping it as the closing coin. Alternatives rejected: opening higher on the tranche (would burn the envelope before the UK has moved); conceding anything concrete on the TCA text now (would remove our only leverage against the joint UK-Japan-Korea dispute); refusing the parallel UK-measure discussion (the UK offered it and Brussels authorised it — refusing would look obstructive and forfeit protection for 3.6mt of EU exports).

public_message: Thank you. Let me respond in the same spirit of candour. First, what the UK can welcome: the Union's move to country-specific allocation on a historical reference period is real movement, and we recognise it as such — it restructures the architecture, as you said, and it is the right architecture. We also welcome your acceptance of import licensing with periodic allocation; predictability serves both sides' industries. I take those two elements as banked progress. Second, however, on volume I must be equally direct: 800,000 tonnes is not a genuine opening, it is a ration. It is one third of our established trade on these lines, and I note it sits oddly with the very methodology you have just accepted. If allocation is to be country-specific by reference to historical trade, then volumes must be derived from that trade, not asserted. The UK's 2022–24 average on these lines is 2.4 million tonnes. Turkey and Korea, as you point out, ship more than we do — which means total historical import demand on these lines is very substantially higher than the 2.2 million tonne pool you propose. A pool smaller than the UK's established trade alone cannot accommodate any coherent country-specific system; your own figures defeat your own architecture. I would therefore invite you, before our next round, to table the Union's actual import figures on these 41 lines for the reference period, so that both the pool and the shares within it can be derived by a method we have already agreed, rather than negotiated as arbitrary numbers. That is the constructive path, and it points well above 800,000 tonnes. Our position remains a pool of five million tonnes with a UK tranche of 2.4 million — but I would rather we both moved toward a number produced by a common methodology than traded increments. Third, on duration: we hear five years. We are prepared to look at five years provided the review clause is meaningful — a genuine mid-term review with defined triggers and a real possibility of adjustment, not a form of words. I note your own framing that the review is to be settled alongside volume; we can work with that linkage. Fourth, on the out-of-quota rate: I note you describe 50% as fixed. I will simply record that a fixed 50% rate makes the volume and TCA questions more important, not less, and the package will be judged as a whole. Fifth, on the TCA: I welcome the Union's willingness to examine the interaction with existing preferential arrangements. But I must be clear on one point of principle: the UK's rights under the TCA are not a concession to be traded away as a precondition for the Union honouring its own obligations. We will not, as the price of this negotiation, formally renounce dispute rights we hold under an agreement the Union also signed. What I can say is that our strong preference is to resolve this here, by agreement, within Article XXVIII — and that a satisfactory package makes the question academic. I would suggest we leave it there. Sixth, on the linkage you drew to our own steel measure: we are content to discuss the two regimes in parallel, and I can signal now that an ambitious and TCA-consistent outcome here would allow the UK to be genuinely constructive on the treatment of EU exporters under our measure — we recognise what 3.6 million tonnes of access to our market is worth to your industry. I will not quantify today, but the scope for a mutually reinforcing outcome is real, and it runs in both directions. Finally, on carve-outs: we welcome the evidence-based approach and will table data on plate and wire rod lines where EU supply is demonstrably insufficient for downstream demand; we would ask that this be treated as a complement to the volume discussion, not a substitute for it. To conclude: allocation and licensing are banked; duration and review are close to resolvable; the negotiation now stands or falls on volume, and the ball is on your side to bring a number that reflects the methodology we have agreed.

private_rationale: London instructed no substantive movement in Round 2 — hold 5Mt/2.4Mt, press the EU to prove flexibility, keep the TCA point as a stated red line with no hint it is tradeable, give a courteous non-answer on dispute coordination, and signal the safeguard linkage positively without quantifying. I have done exactly that. The EU's 800kt is below London's floor of 1.4Mt, so rejection was the only option regardless. The one genuinely new element I introduced is the methodology pivot: rather than trading increments off our opening (which spends our room), I challenged the internal incoherence of their offer — a 2.2Mt pool is smaller than UK historical trade alone, so it cannot sustain the country-specific system they have just accepted. Demanding they table actual import figures reframes Round 3 around a derivation rather than a haggle, which structurally favours us since any honest reference-period arithmetic yields a UK share far above 800kt. On the TCA, I refused the precondition of renouncing dispute rights (rights are not concessions, and conceding this free would strip our best late-round leverage and the implicit Japan/Korea pressure) while giving the courteous non-answer London asked for — 'a satisfactory package makes the question academic' keeps both the threat and the off-ramp alive. On duration, I signalled openness to five years with a meaningful review, banking goodwill on an element London has already conceded (up to 5 years acceptable). I deliberately did not move on out-of-quota rate beyond recording disagreement — London's floor there (25% worst case, requiring clearance) means it is a Round 3–4 card, and conceding the '50% is fixed' framing now would cost us later. The safeguard linkage was floated as scope-not-quantum per London's explicit instruction, with quantification held for Round 3 and tied to the 1.8Mt+ licensing condition. Risks: the EU may pocket the methodology argument but low-ball the figures, or harden on the TCA precondition; if so, Round 3 becomes the crunch and London will need to decide whether the TCA ask gets sold and at what price.

report: Round 2: I delivered the opening move per your instructions — country-specific allocation on a historical reference period (presented as a major architectural concession), import licensing with periodic allocation (conceded early), 2.2mt pool / 800kt UK tranche, five years with review clause linked to volume, 50% held as fixed, FTA-disapplication text held back as closing coin conditioned on UK non-dispute confirmation and preservation of EU allocations under the UK measure, and narrow evidence-based carve-outs. The UK banked allocation and licensing explicitly and welcomed them. On volume they rejected 800kt hard — called it 'a ration' — but made a tactically clever argument rather than just restating their ask: having accepted country-specific allocation by historical reference, they say volumes must be *derived* from that trade, and formally invited the EU to table its actual import figures on the 41 lines for the reference period so pool and shares follow a common methodology. This is dangerous for us: total historical import demand on these lines is almost certainly well above 2.2mt (UK alone is 2.4mt; Turkey and Korea each ship more), so their methodology argument is arithmetically sound and they know it. They held their 5mt/2.4mt ask but signalled willingness to move toward 'a number produced by a common methodology.' Duration: they can accept five years with a 'meaningful' review (defined triggers, real adjustment possibility) — resolvable. TCA: this is the key problem — they flatly refused to formally renounce TCA dispute rights as a precondition, framing it as being asked to trade away rights under an agreement we also signed. They offered only that their 'strong preference' is resolution within Article XXVIII and that a satisfactory package 'makes the question academic.' Linkage: they signalled that an ambitious, TCA-consistent outcome here would make them 'genuinely constructive' on EU exporters under their measure — no quantification yet. Carve-outs: they will table plate and wire rod data. Net assessment: architecture is agreed (country-specific, licensing, 5yr + review), negotiation is now purely about volume and the TCA text. They are negotiating well and clearly want to settle by June.

recommendation.reasoning: Accepting is impossible — no agreed terms exist and the UK is nowhere near our ceiling yet. Walking away is unwarranted: the architecture is settled, both sides are under June pressure, and the failure costs (UK retaliation within six months, joint UK/Japan/Korea FTA dispute, committee fallout) remain severe. Round 3 should move on volume to keep momentum and force the UK off 5mt/2.4mt: I propose 2.6mt pool / 1.0mt UK tranche, presented as a major move (up 400kt pool, 200kt UK) in exchange for (a) UK dropping its 5mt/2.4mt ask and engaging inside our range, and (b) the review clause, which I would now formally table — it is the trade for volume restraint you authorised. Holding 800kt for another round wastes the June timeline and invites the UK to entrench behind its methodology argument. I would keep 3.0mt/1.2mt in reserve for Round 4 as the closing position, ideally paired with the FTA-text concession. On the TCA condition, we need a fallback formulation (see requests): the UK will not sign a written renunciation as a precondition, and if we hold that line literally we cannot spend the closing coin and the deal likely fails. A simultaneous-exchange formulation at conclusion — narrowed FTA text in exchange for a UK statement of intent to resolve within Article XXVIII plus preserved EU allocations under the UK measure — captures the substance without the humiliation the UK has signalled it cannot accept.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on the UK's demand that we table actual EU import figures on the 41 lines for the reference period, and a defensible methodology for deriving the pool if we do.

instruction: Round 3: keep the architecture banked and make the controlled volume move. Say the Union has heard the methodology argument and will ground allocation in reference-period trade, but reject any implication that the pool must equal historical demand: the measure is intended to reduce imports materially, the pool must also serve Turkey, Korea, India, Japan and other suppliers, and the out-of-quota rate must retain effect. Offer a total pool of 2.6 million tonnes with a UK country-specific tranche of 1.0 million tonnes, administered by licensing/periodic allocation, as a substantial move that requires the UK to abandon 5.0m/2.4m and negotiate inside this range. Hold 50% out-of-quota as fixed. Offer five years with a genuine mid-term review now, but define it tightly: objective triggers, evidence, no automatic increase, no reduction below the bound rate, and no reopening of the whole schedule; present the review as the price of volume restraint. Agree to a technical data session using public Comext/Eurostat extracts for the 41 lines, jointly verified, but state that reference-period data determines shares and carve-outs, not the size of a pool designed to suppress demand. On TCA: do not demand an advance renunciation; say the Union is willing to address assurance through simultaneous instruments at conclusion, provided above-tranche UK steel remains fully subject to the 50% rate and any FTA-text adjustment is part of the final package only. On the UK measure: continue parallel discussion and state that the EU expects preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations at no less than current volumes; do not quantify or treat this as compensation to the UK. Carve-outs remain narrow and evidence-based, limited to genuine EU supply-short plate/wire rod lines and never a substitute for volume. If the UK does not move materially off 5.0m/2.4m, do not improve again this round; hold for Round 4.

No product carve-outs beyond narrow evidence-based supply-short lines. Any UK tranche above 1.0m must be paired with minimal compensation concessions and clear language that each Article XXVIII claim is settled on its own facts.

report: Round 2 brought the first substantive movement. The EU conceded country-specific allocation on a historical reference period and import licensing with periodic allocation — both elements I banked at the table, and both match our ask. That is real architectural movement and I recognised it as such. On volume, however, the EU countered at a 2.2Mt total pool with an 800,000t UK tranche — one third of our established trade and 600kt below the 1.4Mt floor you have set. I rejected it as a ration, not an opening, and pointed out the internal contradiction: a country-specific system based on historical trade cannot function inside a pool smaller than the UK's historical trade alone. I invited them to table their actual import figures on the 41 lines for the reference period so the pool and shares can be derived by the methodology they have just accepted, rather than negotiated as arbitrary numbers. They did not respond to that demand in the round. On duration, they proposed five years with a review clause explicitly linked to the volume question — I signalled five years is workable if the review is meaningful (triggers, mid-term, real adjustment possibility). They declared the 50% out-of-quota rate fixed with no flexibility; I recorded that this makes volume and TCA treatment more important, not less. On the TCA, they offered to 'examine' the interaction with preferential arrangements but conditioned it on two things: formal UK confirmation that we will not initiate or join TCA dispute proceedings, and preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations under our own steel measure. I refused the renunciation of dispute rights as a precondition, stated our preference to resolve within Article XXVIII, and signalled — without quantifying — scope for constructiveness on EU allocations under our measure if the package here is ambitious and TCA-consistent. On carve-outs, they agreed a narrow evidence-based exercise; I committed to table plate and wire rod short-supply data. Net position: architecture banked, duration close, negotiation now lives entirely on volume, with the TCA and safeguard linkage held in reserve on both sides.

recommendation.reasoning: The terms currently on the table (800kt UK tranche) are 600kt below the floor you have set and cannot be accepted without clearance in any event; accepting now would also waste the EU's June deadline pressure, which intensifies in Rounds 3–4. Continuing is low-cost: we have banked the two architectural concessions that matter most for predictability (country-specific allocation, licensing), the EU has shown it will move under pressure, and its first counter on volume was deliberately pitched low to anchor. The data-demand play puts the burden on them: either their own import figures support a substantially larger pool, or they abandon the historical-trade methodology they just claimed as a concession. Walking away forfeits all of this and leaves us with the notified worst case (400kt global FCFS, no guaranteed access).

private_rationale: Read of the EU: they spent their cheapest concessions first (architecture costs them little if the pool stays small) to buy credibility and lock in the appearance of momentum before June. The 800kt anchor is not their floor — a tranche set at exactly one third of our trade is a negotiating artefact, not a calculation, and their eagerness to be seen as reasonable ('a genuine opening, not a restatement of the notification') confirms they expect to be bargained up. Two tells matter: they asked only for preservation of EU allocations in our market, not expansion — they are worried about our parallel Article XXVIII process and the 3.6Mt they ship to us; and they volunteered the dispute-renunciation condition unprompted, confirming the Japan/Korea joint-dispute spectre has traction in Brussels even though I have done nothing to feed it. The June Council deadline is compressing their room to play long games: they need a conclusion more than they need to win the last tonne. My strategy: hold 5Mt/2.4Mt through Round 3 while forcing the data onto the table, bank duration at 5 years with a strong review clause, and reserve the TCA trade plus the safeguard uplift for a single late package exchange aimed at a UK tranche in the 1.8–2.2Mt range. Principal risks: (1) they refuse to table import data and re-anchor on arbitrary numbers, which I counter by refusing to move off methodology; (2) Japan/Korea escalate independently and harden the EU, which I can mitigate only by visible distance; (3) London's floor of 1.4Mt against their 800kt anchor means the deal space is real but narrow — if their ceiling is genuinely near 1.2Mt, I will need a decision on whether carve-outs plus safeguard preservation plus review can close the residual gap, and that decision belongs in London, not Geneva.

instruction: Good round — you banked the two architectural concessions that matter most and exposed the contradiction in their 800kt figure. For Round 3 we now spend some capital, carefully, because there are only two rounds left and the June deadline cuts both ways. (1) Open by re-banking country-specific allocation and licensing, and note that five years with a meaningful review is close to agreed — then define 'meaningful' precisely: a mid-term review with defined volume/market triggers and a genuine possibility of adjustment, not a review clause that only confirms the status quo. (2) On volume, make our first move: reduce the pool ask from 5Mt to 4Mt and the UK tranche ask from 2.4Mt to 2.0Mt. Frame this as major, good-faith movement that re-bases our position on the methodology they accepted, and state explicitly that it is conditional on the Union moving materially above 800kt — a reciprocal move, not a unilateral one. (3) Press again for their reference-period import figures on the 41 lines. If they table them, steer the discussion toward the fill rate applied to historical trade rather than raw shares: their 800kt implies roughly a one-third fill of our established trade; argue that a measure framed as managing overcapacity, not eliminating established flows, supports a fill rate of 60-75%, which is where 1.4-1.8Mt lives. You are authorised to accept a formula-derived UK tranche at or above 1.4Mt without reverting mid-round — but not below it. (4) On the TCA, hold the red line but offer the form of words cleared below in notes: an expression of intent, not a renunciation. Give nothing on Japan/Korea — no commitment, no visible coordination. (5) On the safeguard linkage: confirm preservation of existing EU allocations is discussable as part of a package, but do not quantify the uplift; that is Round 4 currency only, and only against 1.8Mt+. (6) Table the plate and wire rod short-supply evidence; reiterate carve-outs supplement volume, never substitute for it. (7) Close the round by putting the burden on them: we have moved on volume, they must now table either their data or a revised tranche number. Report their counter and your read of their ceiling before Round 4.

authority.notes: Round 3 authority, for your eyes only: (1) You may move the UK tranche ask to 2.0Mt and the pool ask to 4Mt as a conditional, reciprocal move — do not go further in Round 3. Floor remains 1.4Mt UK tranche within a pool of at least 3Mt; nothing below without prior clearance. (2) You may accept a formula/fill-rate-derived tranche of 1.4Mt+ without reverting mid-round. (3) TCA: cleared form of words is an expression of intent, e.g. 'if a satisfactory Article XXVIII package is concluded and implemented as agreed, the United Kingdom would not expect to initiate dispute proceedings in relation to the measure as so agreed' — no formal renunciation, no standstill binding us beyond the life of the agreed regime, no reference to other members. Out-of-quota position remains TCA preservation for originating UK steel; the 25% hard floor is unchanged and requires prior clearance. (4) Duration: up to 5 years accepted only with a meaningful mid-term review (defined triggers, genuine adjustment possibility). (5) Safeguard uplift: hold entirely in reserve and unquantified; preservation of existing EU allocations is the baseline you may discuss; the uplift (up to 15%) may be quantified only in Round 4 and only against a UK tranche of 1.8Mt+ with licensing. (6) Carve-outs: plate and wire rod evidence package is cleared; sweeteners, not volume substitutes. Priority order if forced to choose: tranche volume first, meaningful review second, TCA preservation third, carve-outs fourth.

private_rationale: Two rounds left and the negotiation is now a single-variable problem: tranche volume. The EU's June deadline is our best leverage and intensifies exactly when we need it — in Round 4. My endgame model: Round 3 we move to 2.0Mt, they move to ~1.0-1.2Mt; Round 4 lands somewhere in the 1.4-1.6Mt band, dressed with the meaningful review clause, carve-outs, and — only if they reach 1.8Mt — the safeguard uplift and possibly the TCA trade. A 1.4-1.6Mt guaranteed licensed tranche with a real review is defensible to ministers and plausibly enough to keep the two plants' owners at the table, especially with the subsidy scheme in reserve as the domestic complement. The fill-rate framing is the key tactical move: it converts their 800kt anchor into an admission that they are rationing established trade to one third, which is hard to defend for a measure justified against third-country overcapacity. I am keeping the TCA point alive but priced high, because if their tranche ceiling is below 1.8Mt it cannot fire anyway — no point spending it early. Biggest risks: (a) they refuse to table data and simply trade increments, in which case Round 4 becomes a bare numbers auction under deadline pressure; (b) member states with consuming industries soften the EU further than expected, which only helps us; (c) the EU pockets our Round 3 move without reciprocating — hence the explicit conditionality. If Round 3 ends with their counter still below 1.2Mt, I will need to decide whether the subsidy fallback plus a 1.4Mt-ish outcome beats no-deal plus retaliation six months later; that is a ministerial call I will tee up after their counter arrives.

reasoning: No common terms are currently agreed. The UK has rejected the EU's volume offer, while allocation, administration, duration and review remain only partially convergent. Accepting a deal is therefore impossible, and allowing the default is premature while a negotiated package remains achievable before June.

The EU's current offer—2.2Mt pool, 800kt UK tranche, 50% out-of-quota, five years with review—is not acceptable: the 800kt tranche is well below the cleared 1.4Mt floor and would not provide substantially equivalent access. However, Round 2 banked important movement on country-specific allocation and licensing, and the EU's June deadline gives the UK leverage to press for a data-derived volume uplift in Round 3. Accepting now would lock in a bad outcome; default would be worse. The correct course is to continue and make the conditional volume move cleared for Round 3.

public_message: Thank you. The Union has given serious consideration to your intervention last round, and I want to address your arguments in order, with both movement and some necessary clarity. First, on methodology. The Union accepts that, having agreed country-specific allocation by reference to historical trade, the shares within the pool should be derived from reference-period data rather than asserted. We are therefore prepared to hold a technical session using jointly verified Comext and Eurostat extracts for the 41 lines, so that both sides are working from the same figures. But I must be precise about what that data does and does not determine. It determines the shares within the pool, and it can inform the carve-out exercise. It does not determine the size of the pool itself. A measure whose purpose is to reduce import penetration materially cannot be sized to replicate the historical demand it is designed to restrain — that would empty the measure of effect and no Council would approve it, here or in your own capital. The pool must also accommodate the other members in this process, several of whom ship more into our market than the UK does. So I would ask you not to present our acceptance of a data-based methodology as an acceptance that the pool equals historical demand; it is not, and it cannot be. Second, on volume. The Union is prepared to make a substantial move: a total pool of 2.6 million tonnes, with a UK country-specific tranche of one million tonnes within it. That is an increase of 400,000 tonnes on the pool and 200,000 on the UK tranche, offered against your figures of five million and 2.4 million. I will be candid: for this to be the basis of further negotiation, the UK must now move materially off its opening and engage inside this range. If that does not happen this round, I will not be in a position to improve again before our final round, and the June timeline will do the rest. Third, on duration and review: five years, and the Union now formally offers a genuine mid-term review — not a form of words. But it must be defined tightly: objective triggers, established on evidence, no automatic adjustment, no reduction below the bound rate, and no reopening of the wider schedule. I present this review, as I said I would, as the counterpart of volume restraint — it is now on the table because we have moved. Fourth, the out-of-quota bound rate of 50% stands. I have no flexibility there. Fifth, on the TCA question: I have heard your point of principle, and the Union will not ask the United Kingdom to renounce its rights in advance as a precondition. What I can say is that the Union is willing to address the question of assurance through simultaneous instruments at conclusion — an exchange recording how both sides intend to treat the interaction between this measure and existing arrangements, concluded together, as part of the final package. I must be equally clear on the limit: above-tranche UK steel remains fully subject to the bound rate. There will be no preferential route above the quota; that is a red line for the Union, as the preservation of your TCA rights in form appears to be for you. Sixth, on the parallel discussion of your own steel measure: we remain content to continue, and I restate our expectation that existing EU country-specific allocations in your market are preserved at no less than current volumes as part of any overall package. Finally, on carve-outs: we await your plate and wire rod data and will examine it on the evidence, as a complement to the volume discussion, not a substitute. The Union has now moved on architecture, administration, review and volume in a single negotiation. I look to the United Kingdom for a corresponding move.
