public_message: Thank you. Let me respond to what I will characterise as the most substantive round of this negotiation so far. First, what the UK takes from it. We welcome the Union's acceptance of a technical session on jointly verified Comext and Eurostat extracts — shares within the pool derived from data, not asserted, is now agreed between us. We welcome the formal offer of a genuine mid-term review, and we accept your framing that it is the counterpart of volume restraint; the package will be judged whole. We note your withdrawal of any precondition that the UK renounce its TCA rights in advance, and your offer to address assurance through simultaneous instruments at conclusion — that is a workable basis and we will engage with it constructively. And we note your red line on above-tranche treatment, as you have noted ours. I will return to that. On the review, since we are close to agreed: 'genuine' must mean a mid-term point with defined, objective triggers — import volumes, capacity utilisation, price indicators — a defined evidence process, and a real possibility of adjustment in either direction. We can accept no automatic adjustment and no reopening of the wider schedule. With those definitions, five years is a number the UK can live with, and I will say so plainly. On carve-outs: we table today our evidence package on plate and wire rod lines where EU supply is demonstrably insufficient for downstream demand, and we ask that it be examined in the technical session alongside the trade data — as a complement to volume, not a substitute. On our own steel measure: the UK confirms that preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations at current volumes is discussable as part of the overall package. I say 'discussable' deliberately, because — as with everything this side of the table — it depends on where the package lands, and I would observe that 3.6 million tonnes of guaranteed access to our market is worth a great deal more than has been priced into this negotiation so far. Now, on volume, where this negotiation lives. The UK moves today: a total pool of four million tonnes, with a UK country-specific tranche of two million tonnes within it. I want to be precise about what that represents. We have reduced our pool ask by a million tonnes and our tranche ask by 400,000 — we have accepted, in effect, that a measure designed to restrain imports will not replicate historical demand in full. That is a significant concession, and it is explicitly conditional on the Union moving materially above one million tonnes; it is a reciprocal move, not a unilateral one, and it does not survive this round if unanswered. I hear you on what the data determines and does not. But let me offer the Union a way through that is consistent with everything both sides have now accepted. Your one million tonnes implies that the UK fills roughly 40% of its established trade on these lines. A measure framed as managing a temporary overcapacity shock — not eliminating established flows from a market economy partner facing the same shock you are — should be sized by a fill rate applied to verified historical trade, applied consistently to every claimant. A fill rate in the range that accommodates the UK's established pattern alongside Turkey, Korea, India and Japan within a coherent pool sits well above 40% for all of us. That is where the technical session earns its keep: let the data produce the shares, let the fill rate produce the volumes, and let neither of us trade arbitrary increments. One million tonnes does not survive that test. Two million does. I would finally record, since we are in the endgame now: the UK has moved on volume, has engaged on review, on assurance instruments, on carve-outs, and on the parallel regime. The Union asked for a corresponding move; it has one. We look to the Union for its answer before our final round, because the June timeline concentrates minds in both capitals, not one.

No alternatives were better: holding at 2.4Mt would have wasted the round and let the EU run the clock; moving below London's instructed ask would have spent authority I do not have.

report: Round 3 was the most substantive round so far, and the negotiation is now visibly in its endgame. I delivered the authorised move: 2.6mt pool / 1.0mt UK tranche, country-specific shares to be derived from a jointly verified Comext/Eurostat technical session (with the explicit limit that data determines shares and carve-outs, not pool size, since the measure exists to suppress demand), five years with a formally offered genuine mid-term review defined tightly (objective triggers, evidence-based, no automatic adjustment, no reduction below the bound rate, no reopening of the schedule), 50% held as a red line, the TCA assurance reframed as simultaneous instruments at conclusion with no advance UK renunciation (per your revised guidance), preservation of EU allocations under the UK measure restated as an expectation, and carve-outs kept narrow and evidence-based. The UK responded with its first real movement: it came down from 5.0mt/2.4mt to a pool of 4.0mt with a UK tranche of 2.0mt — a cut of 1.0mt on the pool and 400kt on the tranche — explicitly conditional on the EU moving materially above 1.0mt, and framed as lapsing if unanswered. They accepted five years in principle, subject to the review containing defined objective triggers (import volumes, capacity utilisation, prices), a defined evidence process, and adjustment possible in either direction; they accept no automatic adjustment and no reopening of the wider schedule. Duration and review are therefore effectively settled or near-settled. They welcomed the simultaneous-instruments formulation on the TCA as 'a workable basis' and will engage constructively — the dispute-renunciation obstacle has been defused by our reframing. On the UK measure, they confirmed preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations at current volumes is 'discussable' as part of the package — deliberately unquantified and clearly contingent on the final landing zone; they pointedly observed that 3.6mt of guaranteed access to their market is worth more than has been priced in so far. They tabled their plate and wire rod carve-out evidence for the technical session. Their new tactical line is a 'fill rate' argument: rather than trading increments, apply a consistent percentage of verified historical trade to every claimant — they argue 1.0mt implies a ~40% fill rate for the UK, which they say fails the test of a measure framed as managing a temporary shock, while 2.0mt passes it. This is a more sophisticated version of last round's methodology play: it sounds neutral and multilateral, but at any fill rate that accommodates Turkey and Korea (who ship more than the UK) inside a coherent pool, it points to a pool far above our 3.0mt ceiling. Where things stand: architecture (country-specific, licensing, historical shares), duration (5 years), review (genuine mid-term, tightly defined) and the TCA sequencing are all agreed or within drafting distance. The negotiation now stands or falls on a single number: the UK is at 4.0mt/2.0mt, we are at 2.6mt/1.0mt, our ceiling is 3.0mt/1.2mt, and there is one round left.

recommendation.reasoning: Acceptance is not yet possible — the UK is at 2.0mt tranche against our 1.2mt ceiling and has not agreed to anything inside our envelope — but walking away now would be indefensible: every structural element of the deal is settled, both capitals are under June pressure, and the failure costs (UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions against EU exporters within six months, reactivation of the joint UK/Japan/Korea FTA dispute risk, loss of the 'discussable' preservation of EU allocations in the UK market, and lasting damage to my working relationship in the committees) vastly exceed the distance between the parties. Round 4 should be the closing move: go to the authorised ceiling of 3.0mt pool / 1.2mt UK tranche, presented explicitly as the final position and as a 200kt move answering their 400kt move, paired with the full package: (a) the review clause as already framed (we can accept adjustment 'in either direction' within the agreed tight definition — it costs nothing since triggers are objective and adjustment is not automatic); (b) the simultaneous conclusion instruments on the TCA — the FTA-disapplication text narrowed or made inapplicable to UK-origin steel, exchanged against a UK statement of intent to resolve within Article XXVIII, with above-tranche UK steel remaining fully subject to the 50% rate (the red line holds: no preferential route above quota); (c) UK confirmation of preservation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure at no less than current volumes — this should be extracted as the explicit price of the final 200kt, since the UK has signalled it is contingent on the landing zone; (d) narrow evidence-based carve-outs on the genuine supply-short plate/wire rod lines, sized from the technical session, as a complement not a substitute; and (e) minimal pre-cleared compensation on other lines, since the tranche exceeds 1.0mt. On the fill-rate argument, I will accept the *form* (consistent methodology across claimants) but fix the *rate* by reference to the pool the Council can approve, not the reverse — shares derived from data, pool set by the measure's demand-suppression purpose. I should also make clear in the room that each Article XXVIII claim is settled on its own facts, to contain read-across to Ankara and Seoul. If the UK capital seat rejects 3.0mt/1.2mt, the fallback outcome — our notified regime plus UK retaliation and probable dispute — is significantly worse than this package for the EU, and I will say so plainly to the Council through you.

instruction: Round 4 is the close; spend the full envelope in one coherent package and present it as final. State explicitly that this is the ceiling the Council can approve and that there is nothing behind it. Pair it with the complete package, all elements conditional on each other: (1) five-year duration with the mid-term review as framed — objective triggers (import volumes, capacity utilisation, prices), defined evidence process, adjustment possible in either direction, no automatic adjustment, nothing below the bound rate, no reopening of the wider schedule; you may accept 'either direction' language as it costs us nothing; (2) simultaneous conclusion instruments on the TCA: the FTA-disapplication text narrowed or made inapplicable to UK-origin steel, exchanged against a UK statement recording its intention to resolve this matter within Article XXVIII — no advance renunciation, and above-tranche UK steel remains fully subject to the 50% bound rate, which is an absolute red line; (3) the final 200kt of tranche movement (1.0mt to 1.2mt) is expressly conditional on UK confirmation, in the package itself, that existing EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure are preserved at no less than current volumes — convert their 'discussable' into 'confirmed', and tell them plainly that 3.6mt of guaranteed EU access to their market is what the last increment buys; (4) carve-outs limited to the specific plate and wire rod lines where their evidence package shows genuine EU supply shortage, sized in the technical session, as a complement to volume not a substitute; (5) minimal compensation on other lines from the pre-cleared list, since the tranche exceeds 1.0mt. report: Round 3 was the most substantive round yet. The EU made its second move on volume: total pool 2.6Mt, UK country-specific tranche of 1.0Mt (up from 2.2Mt/800kt), and warned it will not improve again before the final round unless we engage inside this range. It formally offered a genuine mid-term review with objective evidence-based triggers — no automatic adjustment, no reduction below the bound rate, no reopening of the wider schedule — explicitly framed as the counterpart of volume restraint. It accepted a technical session on jointly verified Comext/Eurostat data for the 41 lines, but was precise: data determines shares within the pool, not pool size, which it insists cannot replicate the historical demand the measure is designed to restrain. On the TCA it dropped its demand for advance renunciation of dispute rights and instead offered simultaneous assurance instruments at conclusion — but declared a hard red line that above-tranche UK steel pays the full 50% bound rate: no preferential route above quota. It restated its demand that existing EU country-specific allocations under our own steel measure be preserved at no less than current volumes. I executed your Round 3 instruction: moved the UK ask to a 4Mt pool / 2.0Mt UK tranche, explicitly framed as conditional and reciprocal, not surviving the round if unanswered; pressed the fill-rate logic (their 1.0Mt is a ~40% fill of our 2.4Mt established trade; a coherent fill rate sits well above that); accepted five years with a properly defined meaningful review; confirmed preservation of existing EU allocations is 'discussable' as part of the package while flagging the value of 3.6Mt of guaranteed access to our market; tabled the plate and wire rod short-supply evidence for the technical session; and closed by putting the burden on them for a pre-Round-4 answer. instruction: Final round. State of play is strong: architecture (country-specific, licensing) banked, five years with a genuine mid-term review near-agreed, assurance instruments offered, their red line on above-tranche treatment declared, and the whole negotiation now collapses to one number — the UK tranche. They hold 1.0Mt in a 2.6Mt pool; we hold 2.0Mt in 4Mt. Our floor is 1.4Mt; their June deadline is harder than ours. Execute as follows. (1) Open by consolidating everything agreed except volume, and table the cleared review definitions (below) as near-final text — this narrows the room to the number and signals we are ready to close. (2) On volume, run the pre-cleared stepped sequence, each step explicitly conditional on EU movement and framed as final: 2.0Mt -> 1.7Mt -> 1.5Mt. Do not table 1.4Mt; that is your acceptance floor, not a bid. If they land anywhere at or above 1.5Mt, close. If they land at 1.4-1.5Mt, close only with the full review text, assurance instruments, and preservation language agreed. (3) Deploy the TCA concession as the closing trade, exactly once, late in the round: if their final tranche is at or above 1.4Mt, you may confirm the UK can accept above-tranche treatment at the bound rate within the simultaneous assurance instruments, using the cleared form of words ('would not expect to initiate dispute proceedings in relation to the measure as so agreed'). Sell it visibly as the removal of our long-held red line and extract their final volume increment with it. (4) Safeguard currency: you may now move preservation of existing EU allocations from 'discussable' to confirmable as part of a concluded package at any tranche at or above the floor. You may quantify a partial uplift on EU allocations — up to 7.5% — against a tranche of 1.5Mt+; the full 15% remains reserved for 1.8Mt+ and will almost certainly not fire. Do not offer uplift and the TCA concession in the same breath; sequence them. (5) If their genuine ceiling is below 1.4Mt: do not close, do not break off. State once, calmly, that you have no mandate to recommend a number below the floor to ministers and that the notification proceeding unagreed serves neither side; invite a final best-and-final in writing, and I will make the accept/no-accept call in London. One calibrated signal of walk-away credibility is authorised; no threats about retaliation, the TCA dispute, or our safeguard — leave the alternative implicit, they can do the arithmetic. (6) Keep Japan and Korea at arm's length throughout; nothing visible.

authority.notes: Final-round authority, your eyes only. (1) Tranche floor 1.4Mt — acceptance at or above is within your authority given the conditions below; anything below 1.4Mt is NOT closeable by you: hold, take their best-and-final, and London decides in Phase 3. (2) Pool floor 3Mt, but you may accept a pool of 2.8Mt if the UK tranche is 1.5Mt+ — tranche size outranks pool size. (3) Stepped bids: 2.0 -> 1.7 -> 1.5Mt, each conditional; never table below 1.5Mt. (4) TCA above-tranche preservation is now formally tradeable: may be conceded only against a tranche of 1.4Mt+ AND conclusion of the simultaneous assurance instruments using only the cleared form of words; no renunciation, no standstill, no reference to other members. (5) Review text (cleared): mid-term review at 30 months; objective triggers on import volumes, capacity utilisation and price indicators; defined evidence process with joint verification; adjustment of volumes in either direction within the bound rate; no automaticity; no reopening of the wider schedule. If the tranche lands below 1.6Mt, tighter trigger thresholds and a shorter (24-month) review point become a condition of acceptance. (6) Safeguard: preservation of existing EU allocations confirmable as package content at any tranche at/above floor; partial uplift up to 7.5% against 1.5Mt+; full 15% only against 1.8Mt+. (7) Carve-outs: press for at least one concrete plate or wire rod line outcome from the technical session as package content; do not let carve-outs substitute for volume. (8) Out-of-quota 50% accepted as fixed; our value sits in the tranche, the review, and the carve-outs. (9) Duration 5 years confirmed acceptable with the review text as defined.

private_rationale: This is the round I am accountable for. The analysis: 1.4Mt guaranteed, licensed, country-specific access — plus a meaningful review, carve-outs, and preserved EU allocations under our own measure — is defensible to ministers and likely sufficient to keep the two plants' owners at the table, especially alongside the subsidisation option; it is 58% of historical trade versus the ~17% effective access the notification would give us, and it can be presented as having tripled the EU's opening architecture offer and forced them off global FCFS entirely. Anything at or above 1.5Mt is a clear win I can sell. public_message: Thank you. This is the final round, so let me speak plainly. First, the Union recognises your move from five million to four million tonnes, and from 2.4 to 2.0 million on the UK tranche, as a real and reciprocal move. It deserves an answer in kind, and today it gets one. The Union's final position is as follows: a total pool of three million tonnes, with a UK country-specific tranche of one million two hundred thousand tonnes within it, derived from reference-period data through the joint technical session we have agreed, administered by import licensing with periodic allocation. I want to be transparent with you, because we are at the end: this is the ceiling the Council can approve. There is nothing behind it. It represents a trebling of our opening tranche and a near-doubling of the pool, and it is offered against your two million — the distance between us is now 800,000 tonnes, and we have closed more of it than you have. On methodology: the Union accepts the form of your fill-rate argument — a consistent methodology applied to all claimants, with shares derived from verified data. But the rate is set by the pool, not the pool by the rate. A measure designed to restrain import penetration cannot be sized to replicate the demand it restrains; a three million tonne pool against total historical demand implies a fill rate applied equally to the UK, to Turkey, to Korea, to India, to Japan. That is the coherent application of the principle you propose, and the package must include language recording that each Article XXVIII claim is settled on its own facts. Now the package itself — every element conditional on every other. First, duration and review: five years, with a genuine mid-term review — objective triggers covering import volumes, capacity utilisation and prices, a defined evidence process, adjustment possible in either direction, no automatic adjustment, nothing below the bound rate, and no reopening of the wider schedule. That element, I believe, is agreed between us. Second, on the TCA: simultaneous instruments at conclusion. The Union will narrow the FTA-disapplication text so that it does not apply to UK-origin steel, exchanged at the moment of conclusion against a UK statement recording its intention to resolve this matter within Article XXVIII. No advance renunciation — we have heard you on that. But the Union's red line stands: above-tranche UK steel remains fully subject to the 50% bound rate. There is no preferential route above the quota. Third, and I will be direct: the final increment of tranche movement, from one million to one point two million tonnes, is expressly conditional on UK confirmation within this package that existing EU country-specific allocations under your own steel measure are preserved at no less than current volumes. You told us preservation was discussable depending on where the package lands. The package has now landed at our ceiling — so convert 'discussable' into 'confirmed'. Three point six million tonnes of guaranteed EU access to your market is what the last two hundred thousand tonnes buys. Fourth, carve-outs: the specific plate and wire rod lines where your evidence package demonstrates genuine EU supply shortage, sized in the technical session, as a complement to volume, not a substitute. Fifth, minimal compensation concessions on other lines, reflecting that the UK tranche exceeds one million tonnes. That is the Union's final offer, whole and complete. If the United Kingdom cannot accept it, the Union proceeds with the notified regime — 400,000 tonnes globally, first-come first-served, 50% bound, no review clause, and the FTA-disapplication text unamended — and the six-month clock that follows will run in both capitals. I would ask your capital to weigh that outcome carefully against what is now on the table. The Union has come to close. I hope the United Kingdom has too.

public_message: Thank you. I will respond in the same plain terms, because this is the final round and both capitals deserve clarity about exactly where this negotiation stands. First, let me record what the Union has put on the table today, because it is substantial and I want it recognised as such. A pool of three million tonnes is a coherent basis for the country-specific architecture we agreed in round two. The review text you have described — objective triggers on import volumes, capacity utilisation and prices, a defined evidence process, adjustment in either direction, no automaticity, no reopening of the wider schedule — is, in substance, agreed between us. Your willingness to narrow the FTA-disapplication text so that it does not apply to UK-origin steel, exchanged at conclusion against a statement of intent to resolve this within Article XXVIII, addresses the most principled element of our concern, and I welcome it explicitly. The carve-out exercise on the plate and wire rod lines evidenced in our package, and compensation on other lines, are noted as package content. And I acknowledge the conditionality you attached: that the final tranche increment was priced against confirmation on preservation of EU allocations under our own measure. I have heard that linkage and I will transmit it faithfully. Second, on the number. The Union has moved from one million to one point two million tonnes. In recognition of that movement, and in the same spirit, the United Kingdom now moves from two million to one point five million tonnes. Let me be precise about what that is. It is a reduction of nine hundred thousand tonnes from our opening, it accepts a fill rate of just over 60% of our verified established trade on these lines within your three million tonne pool, and it is the absolute limit of what I am mandated to carry. It is my final bid, and it is conditional on the package as described: the review text as agreed, the narrowed FTA text, the carve-outs, the compensation lines, and the simultaneous instruments. Third, candour requires me to say this once, calmly, and without threat of any kind. At one point two million tonnes, I have no mandate to recommend this package to my ministers. The distance between us is now three hundred thousand tonnes — the width of one integrated steelworks' output — and I would ask the Union to reflect on whether the notification proceeding unagreed, with everything that follows in both directions and in both capitals, truly serves either side's interest over that distance. That is all I will say on the alternative; we can both do the arithmetic. Fourth, if one point two million is genuinely the Council's ceiling and nothing exists behind it, then I ask the Union to do the following: put its final offer in writing, in full — the tranche and pool figures, the agreed review text, the narrowed FTA-disapplication language, the carve-out lines and their treatment, the compensation lines, and the assurance instruments. I will transmit that document to London with my assessment, and ministers will weigh it against the alternative, as you have asked. I would add one observation for that written record, since ministers will ask it: for any tranche below what I can recommend, the conditions around the number would do the work the number does not — a review point brought forward to 24 months with tighter trigger thresholds, and carve-out outcomes that are concrete and quantified rather than indicative. Whether even that suffices is ministers' judgement, not mine, and I will not pretend otherwise here. Finally, on preservation under our own measure: you asked me to convert 'discussable' into 'confirmed'. Confirmation against a number I cannot recommend is not something I can give you today — but I can tell you that at a number within my mandate, that confirmation would be available as package content, and that ministers will weigh the value of three point six million tonnes of guaranteed access to our market against the whole of what lands on their desk. We have built most of a good agreement in four rounds. The architecture is agreed, the review is agreed, the TCA question has a workable landing, the carve-outs are in train. What remains is three hundred thousand tonnes and a deadline that binds Brussels as tightly as London. The United Kingdom came to close, and at one point five million tonnes we close today. I look to the Union for its answer.

report: Round 4 closed with both sides having tabled final positions but not the same terms. The EU put its authorised ceiling on the table as a whole package: 3.0m tonne pool, 1.2m tonne UK country-specific tranche derived from verified reference-period data, licensing/periodic allocation, 50% out-of-quota held fixed, five years with a genuine mid-term review, simultaneous conclusion instruments narrowing the FTA-disapplication text for UK-origin steel while keeping above-tranche UK steel fully at 50%, narrow evidence-based plate/wire-rod carve-outs, minimal other-line compensation, own-facts language for other Article XXVIII claims, and an explicit condition that the move from 1.0m to 1.2m be paid for by UK confirmation that EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure are preserved at no less than current volumes. The UK recognised the package as substantial and said the review text and TCA sequencing are effectively agreed, but tabled a final bid of 1.5m tonnes within the 3.0m pool, conditional on the same package elements. They stated plainly that at 1.2m Geneva has no mandate to recommend the package to ministers, though ministers could still weigh a written 1.2m offer if surrounded by concrete conditions such as a 24-month review point, tighter triggers and quantified carve-outs. They also said preservation of EU allocations under their measure could be confirmed only at a number within mandate, i.e. around 1.5m. The negotiation is therefore down to 300,000 tonnes: architecture, administration, duration/review in substance, TCA sequencing, carve-out process and the broad linkage are all within reach.

recommendation.reasoning: There are no further rounds to continue constructively, and walking away means the notified 400kt global FCFS regime with no review clause and unamended FTA-disapplication text, followed by likely UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions against EU exporters within six months and a materially higher risk of the joint UK/Japan/Korea FTA dispute we have been trying to avoid. The remaining gap is 300kt against the value of preserving guaranteed EU access to the UK steel market, defusing the TCA issue, and avoiding a destabilising precedent of retaliation and litigation. I recommend Brussels accept the UK final figure of 1.5m only as a complete, conditional package: 50% out-of-quota untouched, no above-quota preferential route, narrowing of the FTA text only through simultaneous conclusion instruments, express own-facts language to contain Turkey/Korea read-across, narrow quantified carve-outs, minimal compensation, and written UK confirmation in the package that existing EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure are preserved at no less than current volumes. If those conditions are not locked, we should proceed as notified rather than accept a bare 1.5m.

The EU tabled what it declared, in plain terms, to be its final position and the Council's ceiling: a total pool of 3.0Mt with a UK country-specific tranche of 1.2Mt, derived from reference-period data via the agreed joint technical session, administered by import licensing with periodic allocation; five years with the genuine mid-term review we had agreed in substance (objective triggers on import volumes, capacity utilisation and prices, defined evidence process, adjustment either way, no automaticity, nothing below the bound rate, no reopening of the wider schedule); narrowing of the FTA-disapplication text so it does not apply to UK-origin steel, exchanged at conclusion against a UK statement of intent to resolve within Article XXVIII (their red line held: above-tranche UK steel pays the full 50% bound rate — no preferential route above quota); carve-outs on the evidenced plate and wire rod lines, sized in the technical session; minimal compensation on other schedule lines. Critically, they made the final tranche increment (1.0Mt to 1.2Mt) expressly conditional on the UK confirming preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations under our own steel measure at no less than current volumes — converting my 'discussable' into 'confirmed' is priced into the 1.2Mt. They stated there is nothing behind this number, asked me to transmit it in writing, and explicitly invited ministers to weigh it against the alternative: notification proceeds unagreed (400kt global FCFS, 50%, no review, unamended FTA text), with the six-month clock running in both capitals. I executed the endgame instruction: consolidated all agreed elements, tabled my final bid of 1.5Mt (conditional on the full package), stated once and calmly that 1.2Mt is below my mandate to recommend, declined to confirm preservation against a number I cannot recommend while confirming it would be available as package content at a number within mandate, placed on the record that below-floor acceptance would require the conditions to do the work of the number (24-month review point, tighter triggers, concrete quantified carve-outs), and asked for their final offer in writing in full. The EU's written best-and-final is expected imminently. Their ceiling claim is credible: a 3.0Mt pool shared with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan — several of whom out-ship us — cannot stretch much further for the UK without collapsing their parallel settlements.

recommendation.reasoning: I must be straight with you: 1.2Mt is 200kt below the floor you set, and you reserved this call to London, as you were entitled to do. My professional recommendation, for what it is worth, is to accept — conditional on the written offer confirming (i) the 24-month review point with tighter trigger thresholds per your standing condition for any tranche below 1.6Mt, (ii) concrete, quantified plate and wire rod carve-out outcomes from the technical session, and (iii) the narrowed FTA-disapplication text and assurance instruments exactly as described. The alternative is 400kt global first-come first-served with no review clause and the unamended FTA text: on any realistic reading of port-race dynamics against Turkey and Korea, our effective guaranteed access under no-deal is a small fraction of 1.2Mt, secured at nothing, with no mechanism ever to improve it. The package also banks value no-deal forfeits entirely: country-specific licensing-administered access (predictability worth a great deal to our sites' order books beyond the raw tonnage), an enforceable mid-term review with real adjustment rights if the overcapacity shock passes, removal of the FTA-disapplication text as it applies to UK-origin steel with our TCA rights formally intact, carve-outs on our most exposed lines, and compensation elsewhere in their schedule. Preservation of EU allocations under our own measure — the price of the final 200kt — costs us nothing we were not already prepared to give as package content; I have not confirmed it, and it remains ours to confirm in Phase 3. I would hold the 7.5% partial uplift entirely: it was only ever currency against 1.5Mt+. Walking away over 300kt protects the industry's pride and exposes it to the scenario you described as destruction; the EU's June deadline was real, but so is their written ceiling, and I see no lever left that moves them further in the time remaining. This is ministers' judgement and I have represented it as such at the table.
